lines.text: Twenty-six gigabytes of AI, squeezed into nine hundred megabytes. And it still works.
This is Samsung's LittleBit. A thirteen-billion-parameter model, at zero point one bits per weight.
Which should be impossible. One bit is a single yes or no. A tenth of a bit is nothing at all.
So they stopped storing weights. No rounding down. No smaller numbers. They deleted the numbers.
A weight matrix becomes two thin matrices, holding nothing but plus one and minus one.
Multiply them, and the original comes back. The big matrix is never saved. It's rebuilt on the fly.
That's how the cost falls below one bit. The information is shared, not stored.
Samsung calls it latent factorization. Then they add compensation, to recover what the signs throw away.
Thirty-one times less memory. Eleven times faster than full precision, by their estimate.
And the quality matches one-bit models, at one tenth of their bits.
This is how AI ends up on your phone, your laptop, your watch.
